To this end, gain-of-function variants of Escherichia coli RodZ were isolated that restored growth and shape to cells producing a hypomorphic mreC mutant. Production of these RodZ variants in wild-type cells increased resistance to the MreB antagonist A22 and enhanced sensitivity to the beta-lactam mecillinam. These phenotypes have all previously been associated with Rod system hyperactivation, and we found that they were caused by substitutions in the cytoplasmic juxtamembrane (JM) domain of RodZ. This domain is analogous to the N-terminus of FtsN known to promote divisome activation via its interaction with filaments of the actin-like FtsA protein. Structural modeling indicates that the JM domain of RodZ is similarly likely to associate with MreB filaments. Our results therefore support a model in which RodZ activates PG synthesis by the Rod system via a mechanism analogous to divisome activation by FtsN.

title: Murine cytomegalovirus m119-118 encodes a new viral Fc receptor antagonizing host Fc receptor activation
content: Cytomegaloviruses (CMVs) encode numerous immunomodulatory proteins to counteract innate and adaptive immunity. One class of immune evasion proteins is viral Fc receptors (vFcRs), which bind to the Fc region of IgG antibodies and interfere with antibody-mediated effector functions crucial for antiviral defense. Despite the established role of vFcRs in modulating antibody-mediated immunity, their contribution to viral pathogenesis in vivo remains incompletely understood. Although human CMV (HCMV) encodes four vFcRs, only a single vFcR, fcr-1 encoded by gene m138, has been identified in murine CMV (MCMV). By comparing and cloning the genomes of MCMV strains v70, K181+, and K181Perth, we identified a frameshift mutation affecting the spliced m119-118 transcript in K181Perth. This finding prompted us to investigate the function of the m119-118 gene. We show that it encodes a second MCMV vFcR, which we named fcr-2. It is structurally similar to its positional homolog in HCMV, UL119-118/gp68, and binds specifically to the Fc part of murine IgG. Deletion of both vFcRs genes from the MCMV genome resulted in substantially reduced Fc-binding to the surface of infected cells, indicating a complementary function of the vFcRs. Functional assays with viral deletion mutants further demonstrated that both proteins inhibit host Fc receptor activation in a cooperative fashion. Although an m119-118-deficient MCMV was only marginally attenuated in infected BALB/c mice, an m119-118 and m138 double mutant attained significantly lower organ titers than the m138-deficient mutant. These data suggest an important cooperative function of the two MCMV vFcRs for viral dissemination and pathogenesis in vivo.

title: Exploring the antibiotic-producing capabilities of Canadian High Arctic bacteria
content: Microbial communities in harsh environments such as the Canadian high Arctic, remain a relatively unexplored source of antimicrobial natural products. In this study, we developed a pipeline for screening and evaluating bacterial isolates cultured from 23 Canadian high Arctic soil, sediment, and active-layer permafrost samples to discover antibacterial compounds. The pipeline incorporated an undergraduate studentsourcing program and produced created a collection of over 350 bacterial isolates with preliminary antibacterial activity. Following dereplication, whole genome sequencing and secondary screening by co-culture assays, five isolates were prioritized to test crude extracts for antibacterial activity. Among bioactive crude extracts from these isolates, the Pseudomonas isolate with the most potent activity against S. aureus was analyzed. Using liquid chromatography bioactivity guided fractionation, we identified a potential bioactive compound known as koreenceine A, a compound previously only isolated from a Pseudomonas from temperate soil and involved in gene expression of other their microbial community. Here we expanded the known antibiotic activity of koreenceine A and confirmed that a {triangleup}kecBCD genetic knockout of the putative biosynthetic gene cluster significantly abrogated the antibacterial activity.

title: A Third-generation Lentiviral Vector System for Flow Virometry-based Analysis of HIV-1 Env and Other Viral Envelope Proteins
content: Individual human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) particles can differ in their envelope protein (Env) despite being genetically identical. This non-genetic diversity can influence antibody recognition and has been implicated in the formation of persistent virus fractions that escape complete inhibition by broadly neutralizing antibodies. Investigating non-genetic diversity in HIV and other viruses requires approaches capable of characterizing antibody binding to individual viral particles. Flow virometry provides a promising tool for single-particle analysis, but a system combining high biosafety with specific particle labeling and versatility is lacking. Here, we developed a third-generation lentiviral vector system specifically designed for flow virometry. Fluorescent proteins were incorporated into the HIV-1 Gag polyprotein between the matrix- and capsid-encoding regions, flanked by viral protease cleavage sites, creating the packaging constructs pLentiFlow-eGFP and pLentiFlow-mCherry. Lentiviral particles (LVPs) based on pLentiFlow vectors were fluorescent and retained infectivity comparable to LVPs generated with the parental vector system despite reduced particle production. We optimized LVP detection on a CytoFLEX nano and defined a linear p24-based concentration range for reliable single-particle analysis. Using complementary controls, we demonstrated that background from the assessed sources accounted for no more than approximately 3% of events within a broad eGFP+ gate and confirmed that the detected fluorescent particles were predominantly membrane-enclosed. As a proof of concept, LVPs were pseudotyped with vesicular stomatitis virus glycoprotein, severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 spike, or HIV-1 Env. Envelope-specific antibody binding was detected using 8G5F11, CR3022 or PGT128, respectively, demonstrating that different viral surface proteins can be analyzed on a common particle backbone. Together, these results establish a third-generation lentiviral vector system for flow virometry that combines intrinsic particle labeling with high biosafety and flexible pseudotyping. The system provides a platform for investigating envelope protein-associated non-genetic diversity and its consequences for antibody recognition in HIV and other viruses.

title: Andes virus from the MV Hondius outbreak is highly pathogenic in hamsters and airborne shed
content: In May 2026, an outbreak of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) caused by Andes virus (ANDV) was detected aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius, sparking public health measures in multiple countries. ANDV infections in humans are mostly sporadic, most often linked to exposure to infected rodents in South America, although small clusters of human cases, like the 2026 outbreak on the MV Hondius occur as well. It is not known whether virological factors may contribute to this distinct epidemiology, and no phenotypic characterisation of the newly emerged ANDV (ANDV2026) has been carried out to date. Here, using an ANDV isolate from a presymptomatic patient from the MV Hondius, we studied pathogenesis, identified sites of viral replication, characterized innate and adaptive immune responses, and quantified shedding in golden Syrian hamsters. ANDV2026 proved to be highly pathogenic in hamsters, causing severe pulmonary disease reminiscent of HPS. ANDV2026 triggered a delayed type-I IFN response and inflammatory response in the lungs consistent with the key pathological features of HPS, and we detected viral replication in both respiratory and extra-respiratory tissues, including the brain. Infected animals mounted neutralising antibodies and T cell responses, the latter directed predominantly against the L and N proteins. Importantly, ANDV2026-infected animals shed virus through multiple routes, and we detected infectious virus in air samplers connected to cages housing ANDV2026-infected hamsters. In contrast, control hamsters infected with a rodent-derived ANDV isolate (ANDV9717869) shed little virus and air samples were consistently negative. These findings consolidate established features of ANDV pathogenesis, while revealing properties not previously described. Phenotypic characterisation of patient-derived ANDV isolates in animal models can strengthen outbreak preparedness, identify markers of disease severity, and support the development of medical countermeasures.

title: LytM family endopeptidase LmdC is controlled by regulated auto processing and proteolytic destruction in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
content: Enzymes that cleave the bacterial peptidoglycan sacculus, known collectively as autolysins, are critical for growth, division and morphogenesis, but their activities must be carefully controlled to avoid catastrophic lysis. Some autolysin control mechanisms have emerged, but we still know little about how most of them are regulated. Here, we report a novel control mechanism for the LytM/M23 family endopeptidase PA4404 in P. aeruginosa, which we have named LmdC. We have discovered that LmdC is auto catalytically cleaved into N- and C-terminal domains that are then degraded by the carboxyl-terminal processing proteases Prc and CtpA respectively. The effects of various mutations on LmdC-linked {beta}-lactam resistance suggested that full length LmdC is the functional enzyme, with its auto catalytic cleavage serving only to initiate its proteolytic destruction. The auto catalytic cleavage of LmdC was inhibited by overproducing a polymer-forming cytoskeletal protein bactofilin homolog encoded by PA0664, which we named Baf, and a protein of unknown function encoded by PA0663, which we named Api (auto processing inhibitor). We hypothesize that Baf and Api could promote a location specific role for LmdC. In this scenario, the dangerous potential for any free LmdC to cleave peptidoglycan at the wrong place would be prevented by its immediate auto processing and degradation. The widespread co-occurrence and linkage of lmdC and baf homologs, coupled with conserved features of those LmdC homologs, makes it likely that regulated LmdC auto processing is a widely conserved control mechanism.

title: Cannabinoid receptor 1 activity promotes microbial dysbiosis by stimulating the oxygen-dependent expansion of Enterobacteriaceae
content: The endocannabinoid system is comprised of bioactive lipids that signal via cannabinoid receptors, which can modulate barrier and immune functions along the gastrointestinal tract. Clinical studies indicate that endocannabinoid activity is dysregulated in inflammatory bowel diseases. Here, we show that endocannabinoid activity promotes metabolic dysfunction within the colonic mucosa, resulting in microbial dysbiosis and exacerbated colitis. Stimulation of the cannabinoid receptor CB1 resulted in the expansion of Enterobacteriaceae within the gut microbiome, a common feature of inflammation-associated dysbiosis. Preceding this microbial change, CB1 activity induced transcriptional signatures of mitochondrial stress and immune activation within the colonic mucosa. This was followed by a reduction in mucosal ATP production and the induction of aerobic respiration genes in luminal Escherichia coli. Genetic inactivation of aerobic respiration in E. coli limited its proliferation, indicating that CB1 activity stimulates oxygen-dependent Enterobacteriaceae growth. In IBD susceptible mice, endocannabinoid activity promoted mucosal infection by an E. coli pathobiont, which corresponded with elevated pro-inflammatory markers. In inflammation resistant mice, acute CB1 stimulation was sufficient to accelerate the infection dynamics of an Enterobacteriaceae pathogen, resulting in exacerbated colitis. Taken together, our data support a model in which endocannabinoid signaling at the CB1 receptor disrupts respiratory metabolism in the colon, compromising the anoxic environment of the lumen that is critical for maintaining aerobically respiring pathogens at low abundance. More broadly, our findings highlight a proinflammatory effect of endocannabinoid activity that can contribute to intestinal disease development.

title: Context-dependent regulation of RpoS-dependent and RpoS-independent gene transcription by Crl during exponential growth in Escherichia coli
content: RpoS, an alternative sigma factor, directly regulates approximately 10% of gene transcription in E. coli. The small protein Crl functions as a partner that assists RpoS in exerting its regulatory role, particularly during the stationary phase. However, the coordinating role of Crl during the exponential phase remains unclear. In addition, whether Crl can regulate gene transcription independently of RpoS is still unknown. Therefore, in this study, we used the RpoS-dependent operon hdeAB and the RpoS-independent operon proVWX as model systems to investigate the transcriptional regulatory function of Crl using RT-qPCR and 3C-qPCR. Since the expression of both Crl and RpoS is modulated by environmental signals, we further examined the transcription of these operons under different pH and osmotic conditions. The results showed that Crl can regulate transcription independently of RpoS and exhibits environment-specific bidirectional regulation. Overall, this study improves our understanding of the regulatory mechanisms of Crl and highlights the complexity of transcriptional regulation.

title: Exploring recurrent urinary tract infection: paired microbiota and culture-based profiling reveals stable dysbiosis and multidrug-resistant, virulence-enriched uropathogens
content: **Objectives:** Recurrent urinary tract infection (rUTI) is increasingly complicated by antimicrobial resistance (AMR), yet urinary microbiome dysbiosis and isolate-level resistance-virulence are rarely examined together across different treatment states. In this study, we characterized both within the same sample in rUTI and in healthy controls. **Methods:** In this cross-sectional cohort, mid-stream urine was collected from women with untreated, treated and prophylaxis rUTI and age-matched healthy controls at four centres in South India. Of 80 samples collected, 75 were analysed (26 controls, 20 untreated, 20 treated, 9 prophylaxis) by 16S rRNA V3-V4 sequencing. In addition, 105 culturable isolates from the same samples were identified and tested for antimicrobial susceptibility (VITEK 2) and phenotypic virulence. **Results:** rUTI groups showed approximately half the alpha diversity of controls (median Shannon 1.07-1.18 vs 2.17; Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.041). Community structure differed from controls in every rUTI subgroup (PERMANOVA R-squared = 0.091, p = 0.004; pairwise FDR = 0.008) but not among subgroups. Mean Lactobacillus relative abundance fell from 29.2% in controls to <=13.2% in rUTI groups, while Escherichia-Shigella rose from 7.2% to 25.0-43.0%. Control-referenced dysbiosis z-scores were elevated in all rUTI groups (community distance: FDR <= 0.003; uropathogen: Lactobacillus index: FDR < 0.001 for treated and prophylaxis groups). Among isolates, Escherichia coli predominated (35/105; 16/35, 45.7% multidrug-resistant), followed by Klebsiella spp. (32% multidrug-resistant); carbapenem susceptibility was largely retained, and multidrug-resistant E. coli co-carried more virulence traits. **Conclusions:** rUTI is associated with a stable dysbiotic state that treatment does not restore, combining Lactobacillus loss and uropathogen dominance with a multidrug-resistant culturable reservoir that co-accumulates virulence traits. Reading the community and its isolates together may support microbiome-sparing, resistance-aware management of rUTI.

title: TFA-defluorinating microbial consortium achieved with analogue enrichment
content: Trifluoroacetate (TFA) is an ultra-short chain perfluoroalkyl substance (PFAS) and a pollutant of global significance; it is persistent and ubiquitous in the environment across compartments, including food, drinking water, animals, and humans. Concentrations in the environment are rising, concerns over the toxicity of the compound are increasing, and there are currently no efficient ways to remediate TFA pollution, as conventional methods are ineffective at scale under environmental conditions. Microorganisms possessing dehalogenating enzymes targeting the structurally analogous compound monofluoroacetate (MFA) present a potential solution to degrade TFA microbiologically. Due to previously demonstrated dehalogenation of difluoroacetate (DFA) by dehalogenases, the promiscuity of such enzymes was hypothesized to be extendable to TFA as well. In this study cultures obtained from an environmental sample of PFAS contaminated wastewater sludge were incubated in M9 minimal media supplied with 33 mM acetate and either 33 mM TFA, DFA, or MFA in an iterative manner, followed by testing in a 30-day experiment. Free fluoride (F-) was measured at 5 timepoints using a fluoride ion specific electrode (ISE). One culture designated MFA1C significantly degraded MFA, DFA, and TFA (two-way ANOVA mixed model, p < 0.05). MFA1C released 11.2 {+/-} 0.7 M F- which constitutes approximately 0.01% of the potential fluoride release from the total 33 mM TFA applied and with the greatest defluorination activity in the first 9 days of incubation. Fluoride release from TFA and formation of DFA and MFA was confirmed with 19F-NMR. Genetic sequencing and protein-ligand modelling identified two candidate dehalogenase enzymes from Achromobacter denitrificans and Stenotrophomonas sp., respectively, with potential capacity to degrade TFA. The findings of this study are a crucial first step towards future potential bioremediation of TFA, and are, to the best of our knowledge, the first to identify a TFA-degrading consortium of microorganisms.

title: A simple platform for in situ DNA-PAINT optimization enables improved multiplexed super-resolution imaging in Gram-negative bacteria
content: DNA-PAINT enables super-resolution imaging with high multiplexing capacity, yet it is rarely used in nanoscale bacteriology. A likely reason is the lack of straightforward protocols and of systematic characterization of imager-docking strand pairs inside intact bacterial cells, whose envelope and dense cytoplasm differ markedly from both the DNA origami in vitro systems used to develop them, and eukaryotic cells. In this work, we establish a screening platform based on RNA-FISH, in which we extend the 16S rRNA-directed EUB338 probe with docking sequences of choice. This allows imager-docking pairs to be benchmarked directly inside Escherichia coli cells and characterized for parameters such as specificity, binding kinetics, and localization precision. We screened 12 different DNA-PAINT sequences and used an optimized set to perform four-target 3D Exchange-PAINT in single E. coli cells. We further applied our strategy to image three effector mRNAs in the Gram-negative pathogen Yersinia enterocolitica and quantified RNA clusters and their 3D distribution. Our work provides a framework and practical guidelines for high-quality 3D DNA-PAINT imaging in Gram-negative bacteria and should facilitate its broader adoption in nanoscale bacteriology.

title: Assessment of antimicrobial potential of cell-free supernatant from Lacticaseibacillus paracasei SRG isolated from the vaginal microbiota of healthy women against uropathogens
content: Among women, urinary tract infection (UTI) represents a major health concern. Approximately 50% of the adult female population experienced an episode of UTI at least once. UTI and recurrent UTIs caused by resistant bacteria are very common in clinical settings. The treatment and management of UTI is becoming more challenging because of the rise in antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Lactobacillus spp are the dominant bacterial genus in urinary and vaginal microbiota, which are also used as probiotics. In this study, Lacticaseibacillus paracasei SRG isolated from the vagina of healthy women were evaluated for its probiotic-associated properties and cell-free supernatant (CFS)-mediated antibacterial activity against eight uropathogens. The antibacterial activity of CFS was concentration- and pH-dependent, which was significantly evident at CFS/2 and CFS/4 concentrations and acidic pH values of 4 and 5. The antibacterial activity in CFS remains unaltered even after heat and proteinase K treatment, which suggests the role of heat- and protease-resistant metabolites beside the contributions from acidic conditions. L. paracasei SRG showed strong autoaggregation (85.32%) and cell-surface hydrophobicity (55.60%). In addition, it also exhibits co-aggregation with all indicator strains, suggesting substantial interaction with diverse pathogenic bacteria. These observations highlighted the L. paracasei SRG as a potential probiotic candidate developed from indigenous vaginal microbiota.

title: Single-cell-resolved natural giant virus infections reveal conserved protist immunity
content: Single-cell eukaryotes (protists) are key players in microbial ecosystems. Yet, our understanding of how they interact with viruses in nature and how antiviral defenses shape these relationships remains limited. Using a single-cell multi-omics approach, we mapped associations between giant viruses and their hosts and identified active giant-virus infections in an alpine lake protist community. In naturally infected dinoflagellates, infection was accompanied by the selective induction of viperin, an ancient antiviral enzyme conserved from bacteria to humans. We also observed virus-encoded homologs of immunity-related genes whose expression correlated with viperin expression, raising the possibility of a role in viral counter-defense. These findings reveal an ecological dimension of protist immunity and provide a framework for tracing the host-virus arms race across divergent cellular lineages.

title: Glyphosate exposure minimally alters the Corbicula fluminea microbiome while associated bacteria exhibit high tolerance and degradation potentia
content: Glyphosate (GLY), the active ingredient in Roundup, is a broad-spectrum herbicide widely used in commercial agriculture and residential landscaping. Due to its extensive application and high water solubility, GLY is frequently introduced into freshwater ecosystems where it has been shown to negatively impact aquatic life and beneficial microorganisms. The freshwater clam Corbicula fluminea, a nonnative bivalve species widely distributed throughout the United States, is highly tolerant of many environmental stressors and may serve as a reservoir for microbial taxa capable of tolerating or degrading environmental pollutants. As efficient filter-feeders, these clams are continuously exposed to waterborne contaminants, potentially facilitating interactions between pollutants and host-associated microbial communities. In this study, we investigated how glyphosate impacts the structure and diversity of Corbicula fluminea microbiomes and characterized GLY tolerance and degradation potential in individual microbiome members. We found that microbiome taxonomic composition and abundance-based diversity metrics were minimally impacted by glyphosate, while presence/absence-based phylogenetic diversity shifted depending on treatment concentration. Furthermore, high GLY concentrations were linked to reduced Faith''s PD alpha diversity, while other alpha diversity metrics were not impacted. Additionally, we isolated and characterized glyphosate-tolerant bacterial strains from clam tissues and assessed their presence within the microbiome. Several isolates exhibited tolerance to very high GLY levels (up to 1600 mg/L), and several also utilized GLY as a sole phosphorus source and possessed the phnJ gene, suggesting potential degradation capabilities. While isolated bacteria were minority members of the microbiome, more abundant uncultured taxa were phylogenetically related to known glyphosate degraders. Collectively, these findings suggest that freshwater bivalves may harbor diverse microbial taxa capable of tolerating or degrading herbicides, which may contribute to host resilience in contaminated freshwater environments and potentially represent unexplored avenues for bioremediation research.

title: Sister species, shared and divergent responses: early transcriptomic profiling of Bursaphelenchus xylophilus exposed to Esteya spp.
content: Bursaphelenchus xylophilus (pinewood nematode, PWN) responds transcriptionally to nematophagous fungi, but the earliest events preceding cuticle penetration are poorly characterized, and whether closely related fungal antagonists elicit comparable responses is unknown. Here, we compared PWN transcriptomic responses to Esteya floridanum V14639 (EF) and E. vermicola CCF3117 (EV) at 1 h post-inoculation (hpi), capturing the onset of host-fungus interaction. Despite their phylogenetic proximity, under our exposure conditions the two fungi elicited partly divergent host responses at 1 hpi. EF induced a broad transcriptional response enriched in peptidase activity and lysosomal pathways, accompanied by downregulation of cuticle structural components. In contrast, EV triggered a narrower response, without the proteolytic and lysosomal enrichment observed with EF. Direct comparison of the two treatments revealed no significantly enriched Gene Ontology categories, although pathway analysis identified DNA replication and repair pathways, comprising genes more highly expressed under EF. Enrichment analyses revealed a shared transcriptional signature in both interactions characterized by downregulation of xenobiotic- and central carbon-metabolism pathways, suggesting an early reduction in xenobiotic detoxification capacity rather than induction of detoxification programs. These findings suggest that phylogenetic proximity does not necessarily predict conserved early transcriptional responses, although comparisons of single isolates cannot separate species-level from isolate-level effects.

title: Interdependent mode of RNA recognition by the interacting KH-domain proteins KhpA and KhpB
content: RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) are central regulators of gene expression. In bacteria, two KH domain-containing proteins, KhpA and KhpB, are increasingly recognized as globally-acting RBPs, including in pathogens that lack well-studied RBPs, such as Hfq and ProQ. While KhpA and KhpB interact with various RNAs in diverse bacteria, their crosstalk and molecular basis of RNA recognition remain poorly understood. Here, we explored the mutual dependence between KhpA and KhpB in the food-borne pathogen Campylobacter jejuni. We demonstrate KhpA and KhpB interact in vivo, and their individual global RNA recognition is largely dependent on the presence of the partner protein. Using RNA co-immunoprecipitation, we reveal that KhpA requires a conserved KH domain motif for RNA binding, whereas KhpB relies on an atypical R3H domain. Moreover, mutating the RNA-binding domain of one protein compromises the RNA interactome of the other. Overall, we demonstrate an interdependent RNA-binding mode of KhpA and KhpB and anticipate that such KH-proteins have co-evolved to elicit joint RNA regulation in bacteria.

title: Mechanistic prediction of fecal microbiota transplant engraftment and Clostridioides difficile colonization resistance with μODE
content: Shotgun metagenomics routinely resolves microbial community composition down to the strain level via metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), but translating these static catalogs into mechanistic, time-resolved understandings of ecosystem dynamics remains a critical computational bottleneck. Here, we present muODE, a fully automated framework that converts MAGs into dynamical simulations of community metabolism equipped with a composable, literature-grounded ecology layer, fundamentally designed to serve as a mechanistic hypothesis-testing engine. It employs dynamic flux balance analysis (dFBA) coupled to a shared extracellular pool and integrates a composable ecology layer capturing pH inhibition, time-varying antibiotic pharmacokinetics, bile-acid transformations, and spore dormancy. To evaluate the core engine, we cross-validated the dFBA machinery to machine precision against an independent reference implementation. We provide native export to the established COMETS engine for third-party verification. Benchmarking against two independent experimentally validated datasets confirmed that while monoculture growth is robustly captured, overflow secretion and directed community composition remain strictly bounded by the flux-routing limitations of max-biomass FBA. However, when applied to rate-modifying ecological feedback, muODE mechanistically and quantitatively reproduces bile-acid-mediated colonization resistance against Clostridioides difficile. With a single rate parameter calibrated so that baseline deoxycholate matched its measured physiological concentration, the framework reproduced the uncalibrated antibiotic-induced collapse of deoxycholate, with the calibrated inhibitor concentration coinciding with the independently set inhibitory threshold of the pathogen and driving a ~44x shift in the simulated pathogen-susceptibility ratio; bile-acid transformation is represented in the composable ecology layer rather than in the genome-scale stoichiometry. Finally, applying muODE end-to-end to a real longitudinal fecal microbiota transplant (FMT) yielding 139 de novo genome-scale metabolic models, the framework successfully recovered the clinical direction of treatment. By transparently diagnosing the structural competitive-exclusion bias that limits precise compositional prediction, muODE motivates the necessity of community-objective extensions while transitioning microbiome modeling from descriptive taxonomy toward testable, quantitatively-validated dynamic hypothesis testing, laying the essential mechanistic groundwork for the predictive engineering of safe, targeted ecological therapeutics. muODE is freely available at https://github.com/cumbof/muODE.

title: Mice immunized with N1 neuraminidase in a single cycle infectious virus or in a recombinant nanoparticle vaccine are protected against lethal challenge with highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 influenza
content: The recent spillover of highly pathogenic (HP) H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b into dairy cattle and other mammalian species has been concerning. Vaccine candidates that can be rapidly synthesized and implemented are key countermeasures for protecting the human population against emerging pathogens. Here we examine the use of a pH1N1 virus lacking the genetic material for hemagglutinin (HA), limiting the infection to a single cycle (sciIAV) or Cobalt lipid-porphyrin nanoparticles decorated with neuraminidase (NA) of HPAI H5N1 (N1-CoPoP) as vaccine candidates. C57BL/6 mice that were inoculated intranasally with a single dose of pH1N1 sciIAV did not differ in serum NA antibody compared to uninoculated mice. However, mice that were inoculated intramuscularly with the N1-CoPoP alone or in combination with pH1N1 sciIAV had increased N1 IgG antibodies. Upon lethal challenge with HPAIV H5N1, all mice inoculated with either pH1N1 sciIAV or N1-CoPoP were protected from weight loss, unlike unvaccinated mice with substantial body weight losses that succumb to viral infection between 7 and 10 days post infection (dpi). Both pH1N1 sciIAV and N1-CoPoP immunization minimized viral infection such that only one mouse receiving pH1N1 sciIAV had detectable viral titer in the lungs at 4 dpi. By 6 dpi, no mouse inoculated with pH1N1 sciIAV and/or N1-CoPoP had detectable virus in nasal turbinates, lungs or the brain, unlike the high viral titers found in uninoculated mice. Both pH1N1 sciIAV and N1-CoPoP were protective and should be investigated further as alternative vaccine candidates.

title: Species ecology, behavior, and substrate type shape eDNA detection of mammals at savanna waterholes
content: Environmental DNA (eDNA) is increasingly used to monitor terrestrial mammal biodiversity, yet factors that influence detection probability in such systems remain poorly understood. Substrates in and around freshwater drinking areas represent particularly promising eDNA sampling points to capture terrestrial biodiversity, especially in arid and semi-arid landscapes. However, eDNA detection probabilities are expected to depend strongly on the frequency and intensity of animal interaction with the sampled substrate at these watering holes. We combined camera trapping with eDNA metabarcoding to investigate drivers of mammal eDNA detection at savanna waterholes in South Africa (Botsalano Game Reserve) over several weeks during both wet and dry seasons and evaluated the effects of species behavior (interaction intensity with water), species traits, environmental covariates and substrate type (water versus sediment) on eDNA detection probabilities. Camera trapping detected 30 mammal species, whereas eDNA metabarcoding detected 40 species, with 25 species being shared between methods. Body size increased detection probability using camera traps but not using eDNA metabarcoding. eDNA detection was strongly influenced by trophic level, with herbivores exhibiting significantly higher eDNA detection rates than omnivores and carnivores. eDNA detection probability further increased with behavioral water interaction intensity, social group size, visitation frequency, the number of observed individuals, and declined with time elapsed since the last visit of the respective species. A fine-scale spatial analysis within the water bodies revealed that eDNA deposition is highly localized. Substrate type had a pronounced effect, with sediment samples reflecting more long-term mammal activity, whereas water samples reflected more recent interactions and were more sensitive to environmental conditions. Samples collected at wildlife trails exhibited similar patterns, with trophic level and spatial proximity to the trail both increasing detection rates.

title: Interactive effects of land use change and climate drive the decline of a threatened boreal forest orchid in Finland
content: Land use and climate change are two of the greatest threats to biodiversity globally. However, their interactive effects remain poorly understood. In the boreal forest biome, where species are experiencing increasing pressures from forest management and climate change, improved understanding of these effects is urgently needed. Here, we assess the impacts of forest loss and both baseline and changing late spring climatic conditions on the extinction probability of a threatened boreal forest orchid, Calypso bulbosa. We use a unique dataset consisting of 1,006 C. bulbosa occurrence sites located in Finland, historical aerial images, and climatic data spanning the last 60 years. Our results reveal that forest loss, at the local rather than landscape-scale, and both the site-specific baseline climatic conditions and their change over time influence the extinction probability of C. bulbosa. These effects were mainly interactive with greater temporal increase in rainfall ameliorating and greater baseline rainfall exacerbating the negative effect of forest loss on the species persistence. Furthermore, greater baseline snow depth ameliorated this negative effect. We also found some statistical support for independent effects of baseline thermal sum and its change over time, but their ecological relevance was interpreted as minor. Overall, our results align with the expectation that forest loss can modify the exposure of forest-dependent species to climatic conditions, thus altering their vulnerability to climate change.

title: Supplemental water modulates pollinator visitation on resource-rich plant species
content: Urban green spaces provide important floral resources for pollinators, and supplemental watering can improve the abundance and quality of these resources. However, increasing frequency and intensity of drought under climate change create tradeoffs between ecological benefits and water conservation. Manipulating the timing and duration of irrigation may offer a way of enhancing floral traits that support pollinator communities while moderating water use. Focusing on two resource-rich native plant species, Phacelia californica and Helenium puberulum, we examined how the addition of supplemental water in spring and summer affects floral traits and pollinator visitation. We examined mechanisms that may govern the effects of supplemental watering on pollinator visitation, namely the number of flowers, nectar volume, nectar sucrose concentration, and corolla length. Overall, plant individuals receiving more water were visited by more pollinators. In both plant species, this was apparently mediated by floral abundance; individual plants with more flowers received more visitors, though effects of watering varied slightly between the two plant species and the insect visitor taxa. Water additions in spring increased pollinator visitation per plant on P. californica, but visitation rates per flower did not differ among treatments. Responses among pollinator groups varied, with effects driven primarily by sweat bees (family: Halictidae) and bumble bees (Bombus species), while honeybee visitation was consistent across treatments. Our results suggest that insects prefer to visit supplementally watered P. californica plants. Because honeybee visitation did not vary by treatment, supplemental water may disproportionately benefit native pollinators, including bumblebees, which are imperiled. Similar to P. californica, Helenium puberulum plants watered in spring and summer had the most flowers and the most floral visitors per plant and per flower. Spring-watering H. puberulum did not have a significant effect on flower production but did increase insect visitation per flower. Overall, our results emphasize that irrigation and other avenues of water addition are key drivers of flower production and insect visitation, such that homeowners who wish to conserve water must weigh effects on pollinators with the need to conserve water in arid climates.

title: Integrating morphological and molecular approaches to assess photosynthetic species diversity in the Venice Lagoon
content: The Venice Lagoon is the largest transitional environment in the Mediterranean Sea and an important biodiversity hotspot. However, it is under increasing climate and anthropogenic pressures, highlighting the need for long-term monitoring of its biodiversity. Three monitoring campaigns were conducted between 2023 and 2025, sampling seaweeds, seagrasses and halophytes. Samples were identified using an integrated morphological and molecular approach, with morphological traits guiding the selection of the most appropriate DNA-barcoding markers. High-quality sequences were obtained for 50% of the samples and compared with reference databases. To improve identification reliability, phylogenetic trees were reconstructed for each major taxonomic group to assess clustering patterns and sequence relationships. Two independent species-delimitation methods, ASAP and GMYC, were also applied. Overall, 81 taxa were identified, 13 belonging to Chlorophyta, 11 to Heterokontophyta, 28 to Rhodophyta, and 29 to Tracheophyta. We further conducted a targeted survey on Sporobolus species using the trnL-trnF marker and genome-size estimates to distinguish between native and non-indigenous ones. The presence of S. x townsendii was confirmed in the central and southern lagoon, while the non-indigenous S. anglicus was more prevalent than the native S. maritimus.

title: Large-scale exposure of southern seabirds to avian cholera Pasteurella multocida: scavengers as sentinels at different spatial scales
content: Seabird communities represent spatially structured social networks within which potential sentinels could inform us where multi-host pathogens could be present. Pasteurella multocida, the agent of avian cholera, is responsible for recurrent massive seabird mortality events on remote Amsterdam Island, Southern Indian Ocean, but little is known about its broad spatial occurrence. To explore its distribution and whether avian scavengers and predators could be used as sentinels, we screened 18 southern seabird species from 11 islands for antibodies against P. multocida (2634 plasma samples). We detected widespread but heterogeneous exposure among host populations. High seroprevalences were found in widely roaming predators and scavengers (giant petrels (Macronectes spp), and brown skua (Stercorarius antarcticus)), which could represent efficient sentinels at broad scales. Antibodies were also detected over a series of years in a non-migratory scavenger, the lesser sheathbill (Chionis minor) and an abundant penguin species, the king penguin (Aptenodytes patagonicus), suggesting that the bacterium was circulating locally at some sites. This broad scale serological screening of whole seabird host communities provides critical information to assess disease emergence risks in the context of global change.

title: Decomposition trajectories in mixed-species leaf litter in cool-temperate deciduous forest with understory dwarf bamboo
content: Litter decomposition plays a central role in nutrient cycling in forest ecosystems, but the effects of species mixing on decomposition of individual litter species remain poorly understood. We conducted a two-year litterbag experiment in a cool-temperate deciduous forest in northern Japan using litter from two dominant canopy tree species (oak and birch) and the dominant understory bamboo (Sasa). Single-species and mixed-species litterbags were used to examine litter mass loss, litter chemistry (carbon, nitrogen, and lignin), and microbial communities assessed by phospholipid fatty acid (PLFA) analysis. Oak and birch litter decomposed significantly faster than Sasa litter, whereas decomposition rate constants did not differ between the two deciduous tree species. Changes in litter chemistry relative to mass loss were similar between oak and birch but differed markedly in Sasa, indicating a distinct decomposition trajectory of Sasa. Total microbial biomass increased rapidly during the early stage of decomposition in all litter types owing to fungal colonization, whereas the fungal-to-bacterial PLFA ratio was substantially lower in Sasa litter than in deciduous tree litter. Species mixing had no significant overall non-additive effect on decomposition, although mixtures of oak and birch tended to accelerate decomposition, whereas mixtures including Sasa tended to suppress it. These changes in decomposition rate were accompanied by corresponding changes in microbial biomass, while decomposition trajectories remained largely unchanged within each litter species. Our results suggest that Sasa contributes a distinct decomposition process in cool-temperate forests and that species mixing primarily modifies decomposition rates rather than the sequence of chemical transformations during decomposition.

title: Soil nitrogen dynamics in riparian zones of two Arctic rivers
content: Riparian zones act as protective buffers, filtering land-to-river nutrient inputs through retention and nitrogen (N) gas losses. While rapid Arctic warming and permafrost thaw may enhance terrestrial nutrient inputs to aquatic systems, comprehensive assessments of N cycling in Arctic riparian soils are lacking. Conventionally, these zones are considered inactive due to N limitation of Arctic soils and low temperatures, leaving their N cycling unexplored. To address this, we investigated N pools and turnover processes in riparian zones of two Arctic rivers in Finland and Greenland. We combined measurements of the extractable N pool and in-situ nitrous oxide (N2O) flux with 15N-labeling techniques to quantify gross mineralization, nitrification, potential denitrification, and potential dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium (DNRA). Our findings reveal that mineral N cycling in high-latitude riparian zones is more active than previously assumed. Despite low temperatures and low to intermediate soil organic carbon content, we found high gross N mineralization rates, alongside detectable rates of gross nitrification and potential DNRA. We attribute the unexpectedly high N activity in C-poor soils to low C/N ratios, which create a stoichiometric imbalance, thereby enhancing N mineralization. The presence or absence of vegetation largely determined the dominance and magnitude of these pathways. While dense vascular plant cover was associated with higher extractable N pools and gross mineralization rate, low nitrification rates and elevated DNRA potential indicated a tight N cycle. Conversely, sparsely vegetated patches with cryptogamic biocrusts acted as N2O hotspots. In bare sandy soils adjacent to the river, we found high gross nitrification rate and detectable N2O losses, possibly driven by riverine organic N inputs. Taken together, this research shows that Arctic riparian zones may play an important role in reducing terrestrial N inputs to the rivers, which should be considered when studying the fate of N in the rapidly changing Arctic.

title: From tropical rainforests to scorching deserts: biogeography shapes climate-change plasticity in Australian rainbowfishes
content: Thermal tolerance and the plasticity of regulatory mechanisms are likely to influence biodiversity persistence under global warming. Continental-scale assessments of physiological resilience and gene expression plasticity within a closely related clade are rare, yet they could reveal how bioregional climatic history shapes vulnerability to climate warming. We used a comparative approach across five climatic ecotypes of Australian rainbowfishes (tropical rainforest, tropical savannah, subtropical, desert, and temperate) to investigate variation in thermal tolerance and gene expression plasticity in response to warming. We reconstructed phylogenetic relationships among these ecotypes, estimated their ecological niches and environmental warming tolerance, and experimentally measured CTMAX and global gene expression responses to a projected summer heat event. Closely related ecotypes showed divergent bioclimatic niches, contrasting sensitivities to warming, and extensive but idiosyncratic expression responses to heat stress. Plastic responses to warming, including in key heat stress genes, were positively associated with thermal tolerance across ecotypes. The tropical savannah and subtropical ecotypes, both from environmentally variable bioregions, showed extensive transcriptional responses to warming and high thermal tolerance. The desert ecotype was intermediate for both traits, whereas the temperate ecotype showed the most limited transcriptional response and lowest thermal tolerance. In contrast, the tropical rainforest ecotype showed limited plasticity, potentially reflecting local adaptation to milder, more stable conditions and more specialised thermal responses. Our findings support the hypothesis that bioregional climatic history shapes broad patterns of climate resilience, including thermal tolerance and transcriptional plasticity, and may influence which combinations of traits are favoured under future climates.

title: Two decades of Novel Ecosystems: Literature analysis of topics, trends and connectivity
content: 1. As human-driven climate change and other anthropogenic forces produce widespread impacts on biodiversity and ecosystem functioning, many ecosystems are shifting into unprecedented, novel states. The Novel Ecosystem Concept (NEC), formalized in 2006, was developed as an alternative framework for managing "novel ecosystems", human-altered systems that are challenging to restore to their historical state. In the years since, the NEC has been proposed as a broader lens for ecosystem management under ongoing global change. 2. We evaluated how the uptake and potential of the NEC have been realized over time using a bibliometric and linguistic toolkit. Using bibliometric data from the Web of Science, we clustered 40,914 applied ecology papers published between 2006 and 2025 into twenty research topics based on language use. We quantified the volume of NEC research within each topic, rates of publication over time, and cross-topic connectivity proxied by citations. 3. We found NEC research in most of the topics of applied ecology, particularly invasion biology, ecosystem services, soil research and studies of freshwater, urban and marine systems. In contrast, several major conservation-focused topics, including protected areas, threatened species, and human-wildlife interactions, contained little research with an explicit link to novel ecosystems. Publication rates increased across all topics, although growth slowed over time. At the same time, NEC research became more focused into ecosystem-specific topics, especially marine ecosystems. NEC research across different topics was well-connected by citations, with papers more likely to cite each other when they used similar language. 4. Overall, the NEC does not appear to have expanded beyond its origins in restoration to become a broadly applied framework across conservation and ecosystem management. Instead, the concepts behind the NEC have been integrated into restoration and management frameworks grappling with climate and other anthropogenic change, while "novelty" is emerging as a powerful quantitative variable for measuring ecological change over space and time. Our results highlight the potential value of bibliometric and linguistic tools to deconstruct the ecological literature to inform what we can, or should, do to intervene for benefit of nature and people.

title: Community assembly dynamics in a regulated stream: Insights from environmental DNA
content: Degradation of freshwater habitats, including the alteration of natural flow regimes by impoundment, is a major threat to native fishes. When dam removal is not possible, management actions to recover natural flow regimes can benefit native species, but monitoring community responses is crucial to show efficacy. We used eDNA metabarcoding to quantify spatiotemporal trends in fish assemblages along the longitudinal profile of a regulated stream where a court-ratified environmental flows framework is used to benefit native fishes. At a subset of sites, we also compared eDNA results with concurrent surveys conducted using long-term standardized fisheries monitoring techniques to evaluate concordance. From 59 eDNA samples collected over approximately 2 years, we detected 26 fish taxa, including 8 native species, with 25 taxa resolving to species level using a custom reference sequence database; one taxon could not be resolved between closely related species. Fish assemblages varied predictably along the longitudinal profile of the stream and by season (fall and spring). Diversity indices were higher at downstream sites and in fall, reflecting greater richness of warm-water non-native species. Evenness was similar among sites but shifts in species ranks suggests reordering processes drive spatiotemporal variation in assembly. Gradient forest analysis identified thirteen species associated with spatiotemporal gradients, including both native cold-water species and non-native warm-water species. Overall, eDNA results were concordant with conventional fisheries monitoring but eDNA detected significantly greater species richness through increased detection of rare species. eDNA results align with long-term monitoring that demonstrated assemblage shifts in upper, but not lower stream reaches, and extends the insights into spatial responses, species reordering, and ecology of rare species. These findings demonstrate the value of eDNA as a complementary tool for understanding community assembly dynamics, including responses to stream rehabilitation and ecosystem management.

title: Human-wildlife conflict shows shared spatial predictors across ecological and geographic contexts
content: Human-wildlife conflict (HWC) is a global challenge for biodiversity conservation, food security, and human well-being. Effective management towards human-wildlife coexistence, recognized as a priority in Target 4 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, requires understanding the drivers of HWC. However, the strong influence of local human and ecological context means that most HWC research focuses on individual case studies, limiting transferability of patterns across contexts. Here, we link local contexts and transferable drivers by testing whether HWC exhibits an intermediate level of organization, in which local predictor profiles are structured by broader ecological, geographic, and taxonomic contexts. After compiling ~11,000 conflict incidents, we construct and compare random forest models across 29 mammalian HWC scenarios spanning diverse species, conflict types, biomes, and continents to identify contexts in which predictor profiles converge. While predictors varied among individual conflicts, HWC scenarios were organized by shared context: conflicts occurring within the same biome tended to have similar predictor profiles, with continent and taxonomic group providing additional structure. Proximity to protected areas was the most consistently important predictor of HWC globally. The likelihood of conflict increased with human population density across nearly all scales and contexts, while distance to roads was also an important predictor in many contexts. Together, these results demonstrate an intermediate level of organization in HWC that reconciles case-specific variation with broader patterns across biomes, continents, and taxonomic groups. This framework provides a basis for scaling mitigation strategies beyond individual case studies while avoiding one-size-fits-all approaches.

title: Long-term Population Dynamics and Conservation of Proboscis Monkeys (Nasalis larvatus) in the Lower Kinabatangan, Sabah, Malaysia
content: Long-term ecological monitoring is essential for evaluating the effectiveness of conservation actions for long-lived tropical primates, yet few studies have integrated repeated population censuses with habitat-change analyses. We evaluated long-term population and habitat dynamics of the endangered proboscis monkey (Nasalis larvatus) in the Lower Kinabatangan, Sabah, Malaysian Borneo, by integrating a landscape-wide population survey conducted in 2025 with previous surveys from 2005 and 2014, long-term monitoring at three representative sites, and spatial analyses of land-use and land-cover change. Standardized late-afternoon boat-based surveys covering approximately 223 km of the Kinabatangan River and its tributaries recorded an estimated 2,420 individuals in 174 social groups, representing an increase of approximately 66% and 72% respectively compared with the 2005 survey. Group sizes (number of individuals per social group) remained largely unchanged despite the overall increase in population size. Long-term monitoring at three representative sites indicated stable population trajectories throughout the study period. Habitat analyses further revealed an increase in natural vegetation and limited conversion of forest to oil palm within protected areas between 2005 and 2025. Together, these independent lines of evidence indicate that the Lower Kinabatangan proboscis monkey population has recovered while maintaining overall demographic stability under long-term habitat protection. Nevertheless, substantial areas of suitable habitat remain outside the protected-area network, highlighting opportunities for additional habitat restoration and improved landscape connectivity. Our findings demonstrate the value of integrating long-term ecological monitoring with landscape-scale habitat assessment to inform adaptive conservation management in fragmented tropical landscapes.

title: Territorial risk of high pathogenicity avian influenza in France is associated with farmed species diversity
content: Animal infectious diseases threaten food security, livestock production and public health. While disease prevention strategies typically target risk factors associated with high-competence hosts or environmental conditions, we hypothesise that lower-competence species can reduce disease risk by diluting effective contact rates between farms. Using spatial statistical models calibrated on three successive French high pathogenicity avian influenza (HPAI) epidemics (2020-2023), we show that greater local diversity of livestock farms, including cattle and pig farms, is associated with significantly lower HPAI risk. Moreover, we show that the positive association between duck houses and HPAI risk weakens as the number of less-competent non-duck poultry houses increases, revealing a dilution effect within poultry production systems. These findings suggest that livestock diversity is a previously overlooked determinant of disease spread and open new research avenues on territorial diversification to complement traditional approaches for the long-term control of high-impact animal infectious diseases.

title: Warming responses of microbial respiration emerge from spatially structured species interactions
content: Microbial communities are the main drivers of global carbon cycling. Yet, predicting their respiratory responses to warming is challenging because the underlying mechanisms remain elusive. Here, we developed a spatially explicit model, integrating single-cell metabolism with metabolic exchange and endogenous heat production, to disentangle the mechanisms driving community-level temperature responses. We reveal that mutualism amplifies respiratory temperature sensitivity compared to isolated taxa, as exchanged metabolites sustain a secondary growth phase with higher respiratory demand, and this phase creates disproportionately large CO2; emissions under warming (apparent activation energy Ea; increases from 0.65 to 0.77 eV). Spatial structure amplifies this further through threshold effects, whereby diffusion limitation shifts from constraining to enabling mutualistic benefits as metabolic rates increase with temperature (Ea; increases to 1.18 {+/-} 0.09 eV). Endogenous heat production drives additional amplification through positive feedback between local temperature rises and resource turnover rates (Ea; further increasing to 1.78 {+/-} 0.14 eV). Collectively, our results demonstrate that community-level temperature responses are not determined by enzyme kinetics alone but emerge from the interplay of ecological, physical, and metabolic interactions. Our model provides a general framework for understanding the combined effects of the underlying mechanisms on microbial temperature responses. Future climate carbon models should incorporate these considerations to improve predictions.

title: When and why spatial structure favors metabolic cross-feeding
content: Metabolic cross-feeding is central to microbial life. Theory predicts that spatial structure favors cross-feeding by affording cells preferential access to the exchanged metabolites. Yet recent evidence shows that spatial structure can, in some contexts, disfavor cross-feeding. Here, we resolve this contradiction by structuring cross-feeding interactions into three dimensions: (i) directionality, (ii) investment, and (iii) metabolic dependency. We then investigated their combined effects using a spatially explicit individual-based model. We find that the effect of spatial structure on cross-feeding is determined not by physical proximity alone, but by how microbial growth depends on exchanged metabolites. Metabolic dependence shapes the spatial organization of cells and metabolite fluxes, and this emergent organization, in turn, reshapes the ecological outcome of cross-feeding. Our results reconcile previously conflicting observations and provide a general framework for predicting and engineering metabolically interdependent microbial communities.

title: Intraspecific variation at the free-living stage of a soil-borne pathogen is organized into an exploration syndrome associated with infectivity
content: Many pathogens spend a substantial portion of their life cycle outside the host tissues. During its free-living stage, the root legume-plant pathogen Aphanomyces euteiches persists in soil either as non-motile resting oospores or actively explores the environment through mycelium and motile zoospores. These two latter stages are critical for survival, dispersal and host encounter. However, the extent of intraspecific variation during these phases remains poorly explored, and it is still unknown whether they are organized into phenotypic syndromes contributing to infection success. Here, we measured eight free-living phenotypic traits associated with mycelial and zoospore stages across 23 A. euteiches strains from distinct geographic regions (USA, Europe) whose genomes were sequenced. We tested whether traits are organized into a phenotypic syndrome linked to either geographic origin, genomic diversity or infectivity. The microbial strains exhibited substantial intraspecific phenotypic variation that we proposed as an 'exploration syndrome' linked to host search. Beyond this general syndrome, we detected sub-structure according to strains' infectivity, geographic origin and genetic group. This suggests that the free-living stage of pathogens may contribute to disease potential. Our results highlight the importance of integrating functional trait approaches into plant pathology and suggest that the identified "exploration syndrome" may serve as a predictor of infectivity in soilborne oomycete pathogens.

title: Revealing parasitoid-pest interactions using multi-marker metabarcoding: a nationwide assessment of parasitism in cabbage stem flea beetle larvae
content: Management of insect pests of oilseed rape (Brassica napus L.) such as cabbage stem flea beetle (CSFB; Psylliodes chrysocephala L.) is increasingly challenging given a lack of effective permitted insecticides. Conservation biocontrol, including through naturally-occurring parasitoids of CSFB, is one of the first lines of defense and the baseline for integrated pest management (IPM) strategies, but we lack a comprehensive understanding of the parasitoids involved and how parasitism rates vary regionally. Such data have traditionally required rearing of parasitoids from their pest hosts, which is highly error-prone, laborious and overlooks instances of multiple parasitism and hyperparasitism. Using multi-marker DNA metabarcoding, including a novel host-exclusion parasitoid PCR primer pair, we assessed parasitism of 1,040 CSFB larvae from 13 counties in England, UK. We confidently identified seven parasitoids of CSFB larvae, with ten taxa present in unfiltered data. Parasitism rates differed between regions, with the north of England having significantly lower parasitism rates than southern regions. Our novel beetle parasitoid PCR primers demonstrate a high congruence with visual detections of parasitoids and a high rate of novel interaction detections. Ultimately, by determining both rates of parasitism and natural enemy identities, these data significantly extend our understanding of in-field CSFB parasitoid community dynamics. This information could guide the enhancement of farm management, especially using network science in decision support systems related to insecticide application, but also more broadly in the context of crop and habitat management for improved conservation biocontrol and IPM.
